summary: Describes a TCP extension, the MD5 signature option, to enhance security for BGP sessions by authenticating each segment. It was replaced by RFC 5925.

plainLanguage.summary:
BGP, the protocol that decides which routes the Internet uses, runs over TCP. Someone on the path could send a fake TCP packet to break the session.

This RFC adds a small option to every TCP segment carrying a fingerprint of the packet, computed with a password only the two ends share. A packet that does not match is dropped.

questions: what is the tcp md5 signature option
how does tcp md5 protect bgp
subtitle: A TCP option that lets a BGP session prove each segment really came from the other end.

tldr.problem: BGP runs over TCP, and anyone on the path can inject a fake TCP segment into the connection. The most dangerous case is a reset, which can tear a routing session down at will.
tldr.mechanism: Every segment carries a 16-byte MD5 digest computed over the TCP headers, the data and a shared password. The receiver recomputes the digest and drops any segment that does not match.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2385 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 5925, which defines a TCP Authentication Option that allows stronger digest algorithms.

facts.label: Room left in the TCP header for options
Extra header size over the MTU

today: RFC 2385 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5925, which defines the TCP Authentication Option and allows the digest algorithm to be upgraded. It was also updated by RFC 6691. The RFC itself calls its mechanism weak but currently practised, and notes that MD5 has since been found vulnerable to collision search attacks.

sections.title: Why BGP Sessions Need Protection
sections.content:
The primary motivation for the option is to let BGP protect itself against the introduction of spoofed TCP segments into the connection stream. Of particular concern are TCP resets.

To spoof a connection using the scheme described here, an attacker would not only have to guess TCP sequence numbers but would also have to obtain the password included in the digest. That password never appears in the connection stream, and its actual form is up to the application. It could even change during the lifetime of a particular connection, so long as the change was synchronised on both ends, although retransmission can become problematical in some TCP implementations with changing passwords.

Finally, there is no negotiation for the use of this option in a connection. Whether a connection uses it is purely a matter of site policy.
sections.plainLanguage:
The danger is not only stealing traffic. A single forged reset packet can end a routing session, and whoever sends it never has to be on the path at all.

The fix is a shared secret that the two ends of the session know and nobody else does.

sections.title: How the Signature Is Computed
sections.content:
Every segment sent on a connection that is to be protected against spoofing contains the 16-byte MD5 digest produced by applying the MD5 algorithm to four items, in this order: the TCP pseudo-header, in the order of source IP address, destination IP address, zero-padded protocol number and segment length; the TCP header, excluding options, with the checksum assumed to be zero; the TCP segment data, if any; and an independently specified key or password, known to both TCPs and presumably connection-specific.

The header and pseudo-header are in network byte order. The nature of the key is deliberately left unspecified, but it must be known by both ends of the connection, and a particular TCP implementation will determine what the application may specify as the key.

On receiving a signed segment, the receiver must validate it by calculating its own digest from the same data, using its own key, and comparing the two digests. A failing comparison must result in the segment being dropped and must not produce any response back to the sender. Logging the failure is probably advisable.

Unlike other TCP extensions, such as the Window Scale option, the absence of the option in the SYN,ACK segment must not cause the sender to disable its sending of signatures. The usual negotiation exists to stop some TCP implementations misbehaving when they receive options in non-SYN segments, but that is not a problem here, since the SYN,ACK sent during connection negotiation is not signed and is therefore ignored. The connection will never be made, and non-SYN segments with options will never be sent. More importantly, the sending of signatures must be under the complete control of the application, not at the mercy of the remote host not understanding the option.
sections.plainLanguage:
The fingerprint covers everything that makes the packet what it is, plus the password. The receiver works it out again and compares.

A packet that fails is thrown away silently, with no reply, so that a wrong guess tells the sender nothing.

sections.title: The Format of the Option
sections.content:
The option has a kind byte of 19, a length byte of 18, and then the MD5 digest itself. The digest is always 16 bytes long, and the option appears in every segment of a connection.

The layout follows the usual TCP option rules. The kind byte identifies the option and the length byte gives the total size of the option, including those two bytes, so the value 18 covers the two header bytes and the 16-byte digest.
sections.plainLanguage: Eighteen bytes are added to every segment: two bytes saying what the option is, and sixteen bytes of digest.

sections.title: What It Means in Practice
sections.content:
Four practical effects follow from the design.

Connectionless resets are ignored by the receiver, because the originator of the reset does not know the key and so cannot generate the proper signature. Connection attempts by a TCP that generates signatures to a port with no listener therefore time out instead of being refused, and resets generated by a TCP in response to segments sent on a stale connection are also ignored. Operationally this can be a problem, since resets help BGP recover quickly from peer crashes.

Performance may suffer. Some measurements of a sample implementation showed that on a 100 MHz R4600, generating a signature for a simple acknowledgement segment took an average of 0.0268 milliseconds, while generating a signature for a data segment carrying 4096 bytes of data took 0.8776 milliseconds on average. These times apply to both the input and the output path, with the input path also bearing the cost of a 16-byte comparison.

TCP header size is affected. As with other options added to every segment, the size of the MD5 option must be factored into the maximum segment size offered to the other side during connection negotiation. The size of the header to subtract from the maximum transmission unit, whether the MTU of the outgoing interface or IP's minimal MTU of 576 bytes, is now at least 18 bytes larger. The total header size matters too, because the TCP header gives the size of the header including options in 32-byte words, so the header plus options must be no more than 60 bytes, leaving 40 bytes for options. As a concrete example, 4.4BSD defaults to sending window-scaling and timestamp information for connections it initiates, and the most loaded segment is the initial SYN. With MD5 signatures that SYN contains 4 bytes of MSS option, 4 bytes of window scale option, 12 bytes of timestamp, 18 bytes of MD5 digest and 2 bytes of end-of-option-list to pad to a 32-bit boundary, which sums to 40 bytes and just makes it.

Key configuration is also a factor. The key configuration mechanism of routers may restrict the possible keys that may be used between peers, and it is strongly recommended that an implementation be able to support at minimum a key composed of a string of printable ASCII of 80 bytes or less, as this is current practice.
sections.plainLanguage: There are costs. Ignored resets mean a crashed peer takes longer to notice. Signing every packet costs processing time. And every segment grows by eighteen bytes, which eats into the limited option space in a TCP header.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the MD5 Weakness
sections.content:
The document defines a weak but currently practised security mechanism for BGP, and it anticipates that future work will provide different, stronger mechanisms.

The weakness in the algorithm has already been noted inside the document. Since the memo was first issued, under a different title, the MD5 algorithm has been found to be vulnerable to collision search attacks, and is considered by some to be insufficiently strong for this type of application. The memo still specifies MD5, however, because the option had already been deployed operationally and there was no algorithm type field defined, which would allow an upgrade using the same option number. The original document did not specify a type field because that would need at least one more byte, and it was felt at the time that taking 19 bytes for the complete option, which would probably be padded to 20 bytes in TCP implementations, would waste too much of the already limited option space.

This does not prevent the deployment of another similar option using another hashing algorithm such as SHA-1. And if most implementations pad the 18 byte option to 20 bytes anyway, the RFC argues it would be just as well to define a new option containing an algorithm type field. That would need to be addressed in another document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is honest about its own limits. MD5 has since been shown to be breakable, but the option was already in use and the number it was given had no room to say which algorithm was being used.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Always 18, covering the two header bytes and the digest.

fields.name: MD5 digest
fields.desc: The 16-byte digest computed over the pseudo-header, header, data and key.

viz.caption: WHAT GOES INTO THE DIGEST, IN ORDER

items.title: 1. TCP pseudo-header
items.text: Source IP address, destination IP address, zero-padded protocol number and segment length.

items.title: 2. TCP header
items.text: Excluding options, and with the checksum assumed to be zero.

items.title: 3. TCP segment data
items.text: The payload, if there is any.

items.title: 4. The key
items.text: An independently specified key or password, known to both ends and presumably connection-specific.
